questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP and how does Java implement each?
questions.title: Four Pillars of OOP in Java
questions.direct_answer: The four pillars are: **Encapsulation** (private fields + getters/setters), **Inheritance** (`extends` keyword, IS-A relationship), **Polymorphism** (overloading for compile-time, overriding for runtime), and **Abstraction** (abstract classes and interfaces). Java provides language-level support for all four.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can quickly enumerate and briefly explain all four pillars
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing abstraction with encapsulation, or giving vague definitions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete one-line Java example for each pillar and connect them — they work together in well-designed OOP code

sections.title: The Four Pillars — Quick Reference
Four Pillars Summary
sections.content:
| Pillar | Definition | Java Mechanism | Key Benefit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encapsulation | Bundle data + methods, hide state | private + getters/setters | Data protection, maintainability |
| Inheritance | Subclass acquires parent's members | extends keyword | Code reuse, IS-A hierarchy |
| Polymorphism | Same interface, different behavior | Overloading + Overriding | Flexibility, extensibility |
| Abstraction | Hide complexity, show essentials | abstract class, interface | Decoupling, swappable impls |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The four OOP pillars are: Encapsulation — hiding data with private fields and exposing it through getters and setters; Inheritance — using `extends` so a subclass inherits the parent's fields and methods, modeling an IS-A relationship; Polymorphism — overloading for compile-time method selection and overriding for runtime dispatch based on the actual object type; and Abstraction — using interfaces and abstract classes to define contracts and hide implementation details. In Java, these work together: you might define a `Payment` interface (abstraction), implement it with a class that has private fields (encapsulation), extend it with specialized subclasses (inheritance), and use them interchangeably through the interface reference (polymorphism).

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding in Java?
questions.title: Overloading vs Overriding — Complete Comparison
questions.direct_answer: **Overloading** is same method name, different parameters in the same class — resolved at **compile time**. **Overriding** is same method signature in a subclass — resolved at **runtime** via dynamic dispatch. Overloading provides convenience; overriding enables polymorphism.

interviewer_intent.testing: This is one of the highest-frequency OOP questions — expecting a clear, structured answer
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up which is compile-time vs runtime, or saying overriding is a form of overloading
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a table format and give a code example for each — show you can explain both clearly and concisely

sections.title: Overloading and Overriding — Code Examples
Overloading vs Overriding
sections.content:
| Aspect | Overloading | Overriding |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Same class | Subclass |
| Method name | Same | Same |
| Parameters | Must differ | Must be identical |
| Return type | Can differ | Same or covariant |
| Binding time | Compile time (static) | Runtime (dynamic) |
| Inheritance needed | No | Yes |
| @Override | Not applicable | Strongly recommended |
| Access modifier | Can differ freely | Can only be widened |
| Polymorphism type | Compile-time | Runtime |
| Also called | Static polymorphism | Dynamic polymorphism |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Overloading is within the same class — same method name, different parameter lists. The compiler picks the right version at compile time based on the argument types. Overriding is in a subclass — the subclass provides its own version of a parent's method with the exact same signature. The JVM decides which version runs at runtime based on the actual object type. The quick way to remember: overloading is static binding — decided at compile time; overriding is dynamic binding — decided at runtime. Overriding is what enables runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?
questions.title: Abstract Class vs Interface — Full Comparison
questions.direct_answer: An **abstract class** can have state, constructors, concrete methods, and protected members — supports single inheritance. An **interface** has no state (only constants), no constructors, all methods are public — supports multiple implementation. Use interface for contracts; abstract class for partial shared implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Comprehensive knowledge of all differences — this is one of the most common OOP comparison questions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're basically the same since Java 8 — ignoring state, constructors, and access modifier differences
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a comparison table AND add the decision framework: when to use which

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface — Key Differences
Abstract Class vs Interface Comparison
sections.content:
| Feature | Abstract Class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| State (instance fields) | Yes | No (only static final constants) |
| Constructors | Yes | No |
| Concrete methods | Yes (any) | Only default/static (Java 8+) |
| Access modifiers | public, protected, package | All methods are public |
| Inheritance | Single (extends one) | Multiple (implements many) |
| When to use | IS-A + shared state/logic | CAN-DO contract, multiple types |
| Real examples | AbstractList, HttpServlet | Runnable, Comparable, Serializable |
| Instantiation | No | No |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The main differences: abstract classes can have instance state — fields, constructors, protected methods, and concrete logic. Interfaces have no instance state, no constructors, and all methods are public. A class can implement multiple interfaces but only extend one abstract class. My decision rule: if I'm modeling IS-A with shared state, use abstract class — like `AbstractList` or `HttpServlet`. If I'm defining a capability or contract that multiple unrelated classes should support, use interface — like `Runnable` or `Comparable`. Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods, which blurred the line somewhat, but the no-state and multiple-implementation advantages of interfaces remain key.

followup_questions: Can an abstract class implement an interface?
With Java 8 default methods, is there still a reason to use abstract classes?
Give a real-world example where you would choose abstract class over interface.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
questions.title: == vs equals() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `==` compares **references** — checks if two variables point to the same object in memory. `.equals()` compares **content/value** — checks if two objects are logically equal based on the `equals()` method implementation. For primitives, `==` compares values directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: This is one of the most commonly asked Java basics questions — expecting precision about reference vs value equality
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == for String comparison — works by accident with string literals (due to string pool) but fails for dynamically created strings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the String pool, explain why `"hello" == "hello"` is true (same pool reference) but `new String("hello") == new String("hello")` is false

sections.title: Reference Equality vs Value Equality
sections.content:
```java
String s1 = "hello";          // String pool
String s2 = "hello";          // same pool reference
String s3 = new String("hello"); // new heap object

System.out.println(s1 == s2);       // true  — same pool reference
System.out.println(s1 == s3);       // false — different objects on heap
System.out.println(s1.equals(s3));  // true  — same content

// Custom class:
class Point { int x, y; /* equals() not overridden */ }
Point p1 = new Point();
Point p2 = new Point();
System.out.println(p1 == p2);      // false — different objects
System.out.println(p1.equals(p2)); // false — Object.equals() uses ==!
```

`Object.equals()` by default also uses `==`. So for meaningful content comparison, you must **override equals()** in your class. When you override `equals()`, always override `hashCode()` too — required by the contract for HashMap/HashSet to work correctly.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `==` on objects: compares memory addresses (reference equality)
- `==` on primitives: compares values directly
- `.equals()`: compares logical content (if overridden), otherwise defaults to `==`
- String literals go to the **String pool** — same literal → same reference → `==` works by luck
- `new String("x")` always creates a new heap object — `==` will be false
- Always use `.equals()` for String comparison (or `Objects.equals()` for null-safety)
- Override `equals()` and `hashCode()` together — required for correct HashMap/HashSet behavior

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The `==` operator for objects checks if two references point to the same memory location — reference equality. `.equals()` checks logical content equality — whether two objects are meaningfully the same. For strings, using `==` can give unpredictable results because string literals are cached in the string pool, so two literals with the same content might happen to be the same reference and pass `==`. But `new String("hello") == new String("hello")` will be false because they're different objects. Always use `.equals()` for string comparison. And if you override `equals()` in your own class, always override `hashCode()` too.

questions.question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance in Java?
questions.title: Composition vs Inheritance in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Inheritance** (IS-A) creates a parent-child class hierarchy — the subclass inherits the parent's implementation, creating **tight coupling**. **Composition** (HAS-A) builds objects by including references to other objects — more **flexible** because you can swap implementations at runtime and avoid deep hierarchies. The classic advice is 'favor composition over inheritance.'

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of design principles beyond OOP basics — this distinguishes candidates who can think in design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking inheritance is always the right choice for code reuse — not knowing the fragile base class problem
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the fragile base class problem and how composition + interfaces give flexibility for dependency injection

sections.title: When to Inherit vs When to Compose
Composition vs Inheritance
sections.content:
| Aspect | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship | IS-A | HAS-A |
| Coupling | Tight (changes to parent affect child) | Loose (independent components) |
| Flexibility | Low (fixed at compile time) | High (swap impl at runtime) |
| Encapsulation | Weaker (subclass exposed to parent internals) | Stronger (component hidden) |
| Multiple reuse | Single parent only | Multiple components |
| Testing | Harder (hard to mock parent) | Easier (inject mock component) |
| GoF advice | Use sparingly | Favor this |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Inheritance creates an IS-A relationship where the subclass inherits and is tightly coupled to the parent's implementation. Composition creates a HAS-A relationship where an object contains references to other objects to reuse their behavior. The Gang of Four principle 'favor composition over inheritance' exists because composition is more flexible — you can swap the composed object at runtime, it's easier to test with mocks, and you avoid the fragile base class problem where changes to a parent silently break subclasses. A classic example of why this matters is Java's own `Stack extends Vector` — Stack is not truly a Vector, and that inheritance decision exposed methods that break stack semantics.

followup_questions: What is the fragile base class problem?
How does dependency injection use composition?
When is inheritance definitely the right choice?

questions.question: How do the four OOP principles work together in a real Java application?
questions.title: OOP Principles Working Together in Java
questions.direct_answer: In a real application, all four OOP principles complement each other: **abstraction** defines contracts (interfaces), **encapsulation** protects implementation (private fields), **inheritance** provides code reuse (abstract base classes), and **polymorphism** allows flexible behavior (runtime dispatch). Together they produce loosely coupled, extensible code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can synthesize the four concepts into a coherent design example — shows maturity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating the four pillars as separate, unrelated concepts rather than as a system
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a mini-design example that visibly uses all four concepts — e.g., a notification system

sections.title: All Four Pillars in One Design
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Abstraction** (`NotificationService` interface): caller doesn't know Email vs SMS — just calls `send()`
- **Encapsulation** (`apiKey` private, `sentCount` private): internal state hidden and protected
- **Inheritance** (`EmailService extends BaseNotification`): reuses validation and counting logic
- **Polymorphism** (`NotificationService svc = new EmailService()`): runtime dispatch to correct `doSend()`
- Together: you can add `PushNotificationService` without changing any calling code
- This is the Open/Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification
- Real frameworks like Spring rely heavily on this pattern for beans and services

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In a real notification system: the `NotificationService` interface provides abstraction — callers only know they can call `send()`, not whether it's email or SMS. A `BaseNotification` abstract class provides the Template Method with encapsulated state like the API key and sent count hidden behind private fields. `EmailService` and `SMSService` extend the base class for inheritance — reusing the validation and counting logic. And the caller holds a `NotificationService` reference, getting polymorphism — the JVM dispatches to the right `doSend()` at runtime. Adding a new `PushNotificationService` requires zero changes to existing code — that's the power of using all four principles together.
